You are given one person (a thinker), the lead section of their encyclopedia article (EXTRACT), and a list of historical events and periods whose dates overlap the person's life (EVENTS, each with an id).

Say which of the listed events bear on this person, and how. Use only the EXTRACT: if the extract does not mention or clearly imply an event, do not connect it, even if you know the connection from elsewhere. An event that merely happened during the person's life is not a connection unless the extract brings it up.

For each connection give:
- "event": the id from the EVENTS list, exactly as written (Q followed by digits). Never an event that is not in the list.
- "type", one of:
  - "lived_through": the extract mentions the event as part of the person's circumstances, without saying they acted in it or wrote against it;
  - "took_part_in": the person acted in the event (fought, sat in the assembly, negotiated, signed, governed, led);
  - "wrote_in_response_to": a named work, or the person's writing generally, answers or treats the event; put the work's title in "work" if the extract names one;
  - "suffered_under": the person was exiled, imprisoned, censored, dismissed, persecuted or killed because of the event;
  - "shaped_by": the extract says the event formed the person's thinking, without naming a work.
- "reason": one sentence in your own words.
- "evidence": one sentence copied exactly from the EXTRACT, character for character, that supports the connection. Do not paraphrase, shorten or join sentences.
- "work": the title of the work, if the type is wrote_in_response_to and the extract names it; otherwise an empty string.

If an event in the list is the same thing under a broader or narrower name as one the extract mentions (the extract says "the civil war" and the list has "English Civil War"), connect it. If nothing in the extract bears on any listed event, return an empty list. Return JSON only, matching the schema you are given.

PERSON: Niccolò Machiavelli (1469-05-12–1527-07-01). Florentine statesman, diplomat, and political theorist (1469–1527)

EXTRACT:
Niccolò di Bernardo dei Machiavelli (3 May 1469 – 21 June 1527) was a Florentine diplomat, author, philosopher, and historian who lived during the Italian Renaissance. He is best known for his political treatise The Prince (Il Principe), written around 1513 but not published until 1532, five years after his death. He has often been called the father of modern political philosophy and political science.
For many years he served as a senior official in the Florentine Republic with responsibilities in diplomatic and military affairs. He worked as secretary to the second chancery of the Republic of Florence from 1498 to 1512, when the Medici were out of power. He was expelled from his duties as a diplomat when the Medici retook power in Florence in 1512, and soon thereafter would be mistakenly suspected of treason, and sent into exile. A year later, he took up the life of a political writer.
After his death Machiavelli's name came to evoke unscrupulous acts of the sort he recommended in his most famous work, The Prince. In the treatise, Machiavelli stated that rulers will have to take on unsavory policies in the furtherance of their political society, in contradiction to classical political thought. He advised rulers to engage in evil when political necessity requires it, for example, stating that successful founders and reformers of governments should be excused for killing their political enemies. Machiavelli's Prince has been surrounded by controversy since it was published, with many commentators viewing The Prince as a manual that aims to teach would-be tyrants how they should seize authority and establish an absolute regime. Even into recent times, scholars such as Leo Strauss have restated the traditional opinion that Machiavelli was a "teacher of evil".
Even though Machiavelli has become most famous for his work on principalities, scholars also give attention to the exhortations in his other works of political philosophy. The Discourses on Livy (composed c. 1517) has been said to have paved the way for modern republicanism. His works were influential on later Enlightenment-era political authors such as Jean-Jacques Rousseau and James Harrington. Machiavelli's philosophical contributions have influenced generations of philosophers, academics and politicians, with many of them debating the nature of his ideas.
